difficultyReason: The main conclusion is embedded as a rebuttal to an opposing view introduced at the start, and is further qualified mid-argument. A subsidiary conclusion (about the regulators) is marked with 'thus,' setting up the classic intermediate-conclusion trap.
stimulus: Some commentators have claimed that the recent decline in lake-trout populations in Lake Everest is attributable primarily to the warming of the lake's surface waters. But the decline began a full decade before any measurable warming occurred, and it has continued during years when surface temperatures have been stable. Thus, surface temperature cannot be the principal driver. The more likely culprit is nutrient runoff from surrounding farms, which regulators have so far been reluctant to address. Until that reluctance is overcome, any claim to have identified the true cause of the decline is premature at best.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surface warming is not the principal driver of the decline in lake-trout populations in Lake Everest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Until regulators are willing to confront the effects of nutrient runoff, claims to have identified the true cause of the trout decline are premature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nutrient runoff from surrounding farms is the principal driver of the decline in lake-trout populations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The decline in lake-trout populations began before any measurable warming of the lake's surface waters occurred.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commentators who attribute the decline in lake-trout populations to surface warming are entirely mistaken about the relevant science.

explanations.correct: The final sentence states the author's overall verdict: until the regulatory reluctance is overcome, no one can justifiably claim to have identified the cause. Everything else in the argument — the rebuttal of the warming hypothesis, the alternative runoff hypothesis — is in service of that final epistemic claim, which preserves the author's hedging ('premature at best').
explanations.A: Paraphrases the subsidiary conclusion introduced with 'Thus.' It is a step in the argument, not its endpoint.
explanations.C: Overstates the author's claim about runoff — the author calls it 'the more likely culprit,' not the established cause.
explanations.D: Paraphrases a premise offered in support of the subsidiary conclusion.
explanations.E: Overstates the rebuttal; the author denies that warming is the principal driver, not that the commentators are wholly mistaken.

difficultyReason: The main conclusion is a hedged normative claim framed as a rebuttal, cushioned by a concession to the opposing side. A subsidiary 'so' clause in the middle provides the classic trap.
stimulus: Ethicist: Proponents of strict liability for accidental harms argue that it deters carelessness more effectively than fault-based rules. I grant that some forms of strict liability do produce that deterrent effect. But strict liability also penalizes those who could not reasonably have foreseen the harm they caused, so it fails to honor a basic moral distinction between the blameworthy and the merely unlucky. For that reason, the case for strict liability as a general principle of responsibility is less compelling than its proponents suppose — even if strict liability remains defensible in certain narrow domains.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Strict liability as a general principle of responsibility is less compelling than its proponents take it to be.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Strict liability fails to honor the moral distinction between those who are blameworthy and those who are merely unlucky.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some forms of strict liability produce a meaningful deterrent effect on careless behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strict liability cannot be defended as a principle of responsibility in any domain whatsoever.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fault-based rules deter carelessness more effectively than strict liability does.

explanations.correct: The final sentence states the ethicist's overall judgment — that the case for strict liability 'as a general principle' is less compelling than its defenders think — and the hedging ('less compelling than,' 'even if...in certain narrow domains') is preserved. The earlier material supports this verdict.
explanations.B: Paraphrases the subsidiary conclusion that supports the main one.
explanations.C: Paraphrases the ethicist's concession to the opposing view.
explanations.D: Overstates the conclusion; the ethicist explicitly allows that strict liability is defensible in narrow domains.
explanations.E: Restates the opposing view the ethicist is rebutting, not the ethicist's own conclusion.

difficultyReason: The main conclusion opens the argument as a rebuttal, followed by two tiers of support — one of which is marked with 'therefore,' baiting readers toward the intermediate conclusion.
stimulus: The prevailing claim that minimum-wage increases always reduce overall employment should be treated with skepticism. Several recent studies of regional wage hikes have found no detectable employment effect, and in sectors where demand for labor is relatively inelastic, small wage increases are typically absorbed through modest price adjustments rather than layoffs. Therefore, whatever employment losses do occur in such sectors tend to be concentrated in a narrow band of firms. Even granting that larger, sudden increases can produce sharper dislocations, the blanket claim that any wage floor above the market rate destroys jobs misstates what the evidence actually shows.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Employment losses from minimum-wage increases in inelastic-demand sectors tend to be concentrated in a narrow band of firms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim that minimum-wage increases always reduce overall employment is not well supported by the available evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larger, sudden minimum-wage increases can produce sharper labor-market dislocations than smaller ones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recent studies of regional wage hikes have found no detectable effect on employment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any wage floor set above the prevailing market rate will destroy some number of jobs.

explanations.correct: The opening sentence — that the prevailing claim should be treated with skepticism — is the author's main conclusion, and the final sentence restates it more forcefully. The hedging ('should be treated with skepticism,' 'misstates what the evidence actually shows') is preserved.
explanations.A: Paraphrases the 'Therefore' intermediate conclusion, which supports the main point.
explanations.C: Paraphrases the concession the author grants before restating the main claim.
explanations.D: Restates a premise, not the conclusion.
explanations.E: Restates the prevailing claim that the author is rebutting.

difficultyReason: Main conclusion is embedded between two subsidiary conclusions, each introduced by its own marker ('it follows,' 'thus'). The author's actual point is a hedged normative claim about judicial reasoning.
stimulus: Legal theorist: Appellate judges frequently cite foreign precedent in domestic constitutional cases. Critics charge that this practice is improper because foreign rulings lack binding authority here. It follows that foreign precedent cannot settle a domestic constitutional question. But judges do not cite such precedent in order to settle questions; they cite it to illuminate the range of reasonable answers others have reached. Courts should therefore continue the practice, albeit with candid acknowledgment of its limited evidentiary weight. Thus, wholesale rejection of foreign precedent is unwarranted.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the legal theorist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Foreign precedent cannot, on its own, settle a domestic constitutional question.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Appellate courts should continue to cite foreign precedent, while candidly acknowledging its limited evidentiary weight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A complete rejection of the practice of citing foreign precedent is not warranted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Judges who cite foreign precedent do so to illuminate, not to settle, domestic constitutional questions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The practice of citing foreign precedent in domestic constitutional cases is improper because foreign rulings lack binding authority.

explanations.correct: The penultimate sentence — 'Courts should therefore continue the practice, albeit with candid acknowledgment of its limited evidentiary weight' — is the author's normative recommendation, with its hedging intact. The following 'Thus' sentence restates a negative corollary; the 'should continue' sentence is what everything supports.
explanations.A: Paraphrases the 'It follows' subsidiary conclusion, which the theorist grants to the critics as a setup.
explanations.C: Paraphrases the final 'Thus' sentence, which is a restated corollary of the main recommendation, not the recommendation itself.
explanations.D: Paraphrases a premise used to support the main recommendation.
explanations.E: Restates the critics' position, which the theorist is rebutting.

difficultyReason: The author rebuts a popular claim; the rebuttal is hedged and sandwiched between a concession and a middle subsidiary conclusion introduced with 'hence.' The opposing view is recognizable enough to trap readers.
stimulus: Many observers hold that rapid advances in machine translation will soon render professional translators obsolete. It is true that current systems can produce passable renderings of routine commercial correspondence with remarkable speed. Hence, the market for low-stakes translation work has already contracted sharply. But literary, legal, and diplomatic translation require judgments about tone, register, and consequence that no present system reliably replicates. So the confident prediction that translators as a profession are on their way out looks, for the foreseeable future, to be overstated.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The market for low-stakes translation work has already contracted sharply as a result of advances in machine translation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Current machine-translation systems can produce passable renderings of routine commercial correspondence with remarkable speed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rapid advances in machine translation will soon render professional translators obsolete.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim that professional translators are on their way out appears, for the foreseeable future, to be overstated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No machine-translation system will ever match human translators at handling tone, register, and consequence.

explanations.correct: The final sentence states the author's verdict and preserves the hedging — 'for the foreseeable future' and 'overstated.' Everything else, including the concession and the 'Hence' intermediate conclusion, supports this judgment.
explanations.B: Restates a premise the author concedes before making the main point.
explanations.C: Restates the view the author is rebutting.
explanations.E: Overstates the conclusion — the author claims the prediction is overstated 'for the foreseeable future,' not that machines will never match humans.

difficultyReason: The stimulus presents a rebuttal of a popular linguistic claim, with the main conclusion tucked between an intermediate conclusion and a final restatement of what has been shown. Hedging ('largely,' 'on the whole') is load-bearing.
stimulus: Linguist: A familiar claim holds that languages with rich case-marking systems permit freer word order than languages without them. Historical surveys, however, show that many richly inflected languages maintained rigid word orders for centuries, while some impoverished-morphology languages permit substantial reordering for discourse purposes. It follows that case-marking alone does not determine word-order flexibility. The popular claim, on the whole, conflates a statistical tendency with a grammatical necessity — and that is the error most worth correcting. The tendency itself is real enough; the necessity is not.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Case-marking alone does not determine how freely a language permits reordering of words.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The popular claim linking rich case-marking to free word order errs chiefly by treating a statistical tendency as a grammatical necessity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is no real statistical tendency for richly inflected languages to permit freer word order than impoverished-morphology languages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some impoverished-morphology languages permit substantial word-order variation for discourse purposes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historical surveys of word order provide the strongest available evidence against traditional typological claims.

explanations.correct: The fourth sentence identifies the author's real target — the conflation of tendency with necessity — and labels it 'the error most worth correcting.' The final sentence underscores the same point. The 'It follows' sentence is an intermediate step en route to this diagnosis.
explanations.C: Overstates/contradicts the author, who explicitly grants the statistical tendency.
explanations.E: Not claimed — the linguist cites historical surveys but makes no general claim about their evidentiary primacy.

difficultyReason: Historical stimulus framed as a rebuttal to a standard explanation, with a 'so' intermediate conclusion and a concession. The hedged final verdict is the main point.
stimulus: Historian: Textbooks typically attribute the collapse of the late-Bronze-Age trading network to a single cause — the arrival of the so-called Sea Peoples. But archaeological records show that several of the network's major cities had already entered severe economic decline decades before any incursion. So these incursions cannot have initiated the collapse. I acknowledge that raiding may have accelerated an ongoing decay. Still, to treat the incursions as the principal cause, rather than as one among several converging pressures, is to misread the evidence.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The arrival of the Sea Peoples cannot have initiated the collapse of the late-Bronze-Age trading network.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a misreading of the evidence to treat the Sea Peoples' incursions as the principal cause of the collapse rather than as one among several converging pressures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several major cities in the late-Bronze-Age trading network had entered severe economic decline before any outside incursion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raiding by the Sea Peoples may have accelerated an ongoing decay of the late-Bronze-Age trading network.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Sea Peoples had essentially no effect on the trajectory of the late-Bronze-Age trading network.

explanations.correct: The final sentence delivers the historian's verdict, preserving the hedging that the incursions are one cause among several rather than none at all.
explanations.A: Paraphrases the 'So' intermediate conclusion, which supports but is not the main point.
explanations.E: Overstates the conclusion — the historian allows that raiding may have accelerated the decay.

difficultyReason: Policy stimulus in which the main conclusion is a hedged procedural recommendation framed as a rebuttal to both sides of a debate. A 'therefore' sits mid-argument to bait readers.
stimulus: Policy analyst: Advocates of the proposed housing tax credit insist it will make homeownership attainable for middle-income families; opponents claim it will chiefly enrich developers. The credit's actual effects will depend on market conditions that cannot be reliably forecast at this stage. Therefore, any confident prediction about who will benefit is unwarranted. What follows from this, however, is not that the credit should be rejected, but that it should be adopted only with a sunset provision requiring reevaluation within five years. A program whose effects we cannot yet forecast deserves neither enthusiastic endorsement nor outright rejection.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the policy analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confident predictions about which group will benefit from the proposed housing tax credit are not warranted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proposed housing tax credit should be adopted only with a sunset provision requiring reevaluation within five years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The proposed housing tax credit should be rejected until more reliable market forecasts become available.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The effects of the proposed housing tax credit cannot be reliably forecast at this stage.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Advocates of the housing tax credit have offered a more defensible position than its opponents have.

explanations.correct: The fourth sentence contains the analyst's affirmative recommendation — adopt with a sunset provision — and the final sentence underscores it. The hedging ('only with,' 'deserves neither...nor') is preserved.
explanations.C: Contradicts the analyst, who explicitly rejects outright rejection.
explanations.E: Not claimed — the analyst rebuts both sides' confidence, not one side's position.

difficultyReason: Arts-criticism stimulus in which the main conclusion is stated at the outset as a rebuttal, qualified by concession, and then restated more narrowly. A 'thus' subsidiary conclusion creates the standard trap.
stimulus: Museum curator: The recent trend of evaluating historical paintings primarily in terms of the social conditions under which they were produced yields, at best, a partial understanding of those works. Granted, such evaluations have usefully corrected earlier views that treated artworks as if they floated free of their times. Thus, the purely formalist approach of previous generations is no longer tenable. Yet reducing a painting to the circumstances of its making is no better; it simply substitutes one kind of blindness for another. A fuller account must, at the very least, weigh formal achievement alongside historical situation.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the curator's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The purely formalist approach to evaluating historical paintings favored by previous generations is no longer tenable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evaluating historical paintings primarily in terms of the social conditions of their production yields only a partial understanding of those works.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Earlier views treating artworks as if they floated free of their times have been usefully corrected by recent social-context approaches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A fuller account of historical paintings should weigh formal achievement and historical situation equally.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Evaluating historical paintings in terms of their social conditions is no less misleading than evaluating them in purely formalist terms.

explanations.correct: The opening sentence states the curator's main conclusion with its hedging intact ('at best, a partial understanding'). The rest of the argument defends that claim through a concession, a 'Thus' subsidiary conclusion, and a proposed alternative.
explanations.C: Paraphrases the curator's concession to the social-context view.
explanations.D: Overstates the final clause — the curator says formal achievement and historical situation must 'at the very least' be weighed together, not weighed equally.
explanations.E: Overstates the comparison — the curator says reducing a painting to its making is 'no better,' meaning not an improvement over formalism, but the answer choice asserts strict equivalence across the board, a stronger claim than the argument supports.

difficultyReason: Medical stimulus with two tiers of reasoning: an intermediate 'therefore' conclusion about the study's scope, and a hedged final recommendation framed as a rebuttal to enthusiastic press coverage.
stimulus: Medical researcher: News coverage of our recent trial has suggested that a single daily dose of compound N substantially reduces the risk of recurrent stroke in the general population. In fact, our trial enrolled only patients who had already suffered two or more strokes within the prior year. Therefore, the results can speak, at most, to a narrow subset of high-risk patients. It would accordingly be premature — and, in light of compound N's known side effects, potentially harmful — to recommend the drug for broader preventive use before larger trials are completed.
questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It would be premature to recommend compound N for broad preventive use against recurrent stroke before larger trials are completed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The trial's results can speak, at most, to a narrow subset of high-risk stroke patients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: News coverage has overstated the implications of the recent trial of compound N for the general population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The trial of compound N enrolled only patients who had already suffered two or more strokes within the prior year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Compound N's known side effects make it unsuitable as a preventive treatment against recurrent stroke.

explanations.correct: The final sentence delivers the researcher's recommendation with its hedging preserved ('premature,' 'before larger trials are completed'). The earlier material, including the 'Therefore' subsidiary conclusion, supports this recommendation.
explanations.B: Paraphrases the 'Therefore' subsidiary conclusion, which supports the main recommendation.
explanations.C: Paraphrases the rebutted view in summary form — the researcher's point is not merely that coverage overstated things but what ought to be done in response.
explanations.E: Overstates the conclusion — the researcher cites side effects as one reason for caution, not as establishing unsuitability outright.
